# Susīmajātaka (Ja 411)

**ID:** Ja 411
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Susīmajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** King Susīma
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja411
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul6.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Susīmajātaka* (Ja 411) is a story belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon [SuttaCentral]. The canonical verse incipit opens with *Kāḷāni kesāni pure ahesum* (“Heretofore the hairs [were black]”) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The framing story is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses the monks in the Hall of Truth (*dhammasabhā*) as they praise his Great Renunciation (*mahānekkhammam*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The Buddha explains that he had likewise renounced worldly dominion in a previous existence, having abandoned the sovereignty of Kāsi (measuring three hundred leagues in extent) [SuttaCentral]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was King Susīma (*Susīmarājā*), who, upon seeing his hairs turn grey, renounced his royal splendour, departed into the Himalayas to pursue the ascetic life (*isipabbajjā*), developed the meditative absorptions and higher spiritual knowledges (*jhānābhiññā*), and was ultimately reborn in the realm of Brahmā [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the chief queen is identified with Rāhulamātā and King Susīma with the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].

DharmaNexus identifies 9 Pali-internal text-reuse matches between Ja 411 and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Vol. 3), covering 1,083 characters with a shared sequence ranging from §1.4–3.4 to §3531_2–3537 (similarity 0.91) [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan for this specific jātaka [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].

In modern scholarship, Jātaka 411 is cited by James George Jennings as an illustration of royal sons being sent away to receive their education at the ancient institution of Takkasilā [Jennings 1948]. Sujin Boriharnwanaket cites the commentary to *Susīma Jātaka* no. 411 when discussing the Bodhisatta's contemplation of the difficulty of giving up sensual pleasures, using the simile of a sick patient who must be assisted by a nurse with a pulling string to rise [Sujin Boriharnwanaket]. However, aspects of the narrative context cited in these modern discussions—in which young Susīma is described as the son of the king's chaplain studying alongside a royal prince at Takkasilā—appear to reflect details from the earlier homonymous *Susīmajātaka* (Ja 163) [Fausböll 1883; Sujin Boriharnwanaket].
